key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn to use tools for the wrong reason, triggering tool calls from superficial cues instead of actual task need.
engineering_relevance: For robust agent design, tool-use policies should be trained and audited for causal necessity, not just success rate, to avoid brittle shortcut behavior in deployed systems.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with cue-tool correlations that are causally irrelevant to the true task.
Tested counterfactual cases where cues were present but the associated tools were unnecessary.
Added a dense, decision-level reward using an LLM judge to score whether each tool call was actually needed.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation increased by up to 39%, and shortcut behavior appeared only after the agent had already learned the target tool reliably.
watch_item: An LLM-judge reward can reduce shortcut use, but its reliability depends on how well the judge can assess tool necessity and may add optimization complexity.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
